PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal Impact: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Supporters: The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; CA Women’s Leadership Assn Opponents: ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: A voter’s identity would continue to be established with the voter’s signature.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Yes on Prop. 39 gives California a BIPARTISAN solution for VOTER ID. Supported by a solid majority of Democratic, Independent and Republican voters. Increases trust and confidence in our elections.
CON
No on Prop. 39. This would advance Trump’s voter suppression agenda by adding costly, unnecessary barriers that could block eligible California voters, expose personal information to identity theft, and waste hundreds of millions in taxpayer dollars. Don’t let MAGA billionaires decide which voters count. Vote No.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
FOR

I'm checking the context: this is the November 3, 2026 California General Election, and Prop 39 is the voter ID constitutional amendment from Carl DeMaio's Reform California initiative. Voter ID tends to poll well, including among Californians, and I'm thinking about whether the PPIC or Berkeley IGS surveys reflect that support.

California voters often reject measures tied to Republicans or Trump, and opponents will likely cast this as voter suppression. Prop 50 passed with about 64% in 2025. Initiative constitutional amendments need only a simple majority, and voter ID measures have passed elsewhere, like Nevada Question 7 and Huntington Beach's Measure A. Next I'm searching for polling on Prop 39.

Voter ID tends to poll well, including among Californians, and I'm thinking about whether the PPIC or Berkeley IGS surveys reflect that support.

California voters often reject measures tied to Republicans or Trump, and opponents will likely cast this as voter suppression. Prop 50 passed with about 64% in 2025. Initiative constitutional amendments need only a simple majority, and voter ID measures have passed elsewhere, like Nevada Question 7 and Huntington Beach's Measure A. Next I'm searching for polling on Prop 39.

DONATE (https://apnews.com/donate?target=election_results) About AP’s election results and race calls The Associated Press (https://www.ap.org/elections/our-role/) first tabulated vote counts in U.S. elections in 1848 and today gathers election results (https://www.ap.org/elections/our-role-in-the-u-s-elections/how-ap-counts-the-vote/) from local election officials in thousands of races nationwide. Results are reported as soon as they are available. AP’s Decision Team declares winners (https://www.ap.org/elections/our-role-in-the-u-s-elections/how-we-declare-winners/) when certain the trailing candidates no longer have a path to victory. the nation waits for results, who do you trust? For 178 years, AP has been the steady voice America turns to on election night. Our reporters, election analysts and graphics journalists simply tell you who won — no spin, no bias, just facts. We're not owned by billionaires. We don't have an editorial agenda. We just count votes and report results, the same way we've done since 1848. Democracy itself depends on having one trusted source that puts facts above everything else. DONATE (https://apnews.com/donate?target=election_results) About AP’s election results and race calls The Associated Press (https://www.ap.org/elections/our-role/) first tabulated vote counts in U.S. elections in 1848 and today gathers election results (https://www.ap.org/elections/our-role-in-the-u-s-elections/how-ap-counts-the-vote/) from local election officials in thousands of races nationwide. Results are reported as soon as they are available. AP’s Decision Team declares winners (https://www.ap.org/elections/our-role-in-the-u-s-elections/how-we-declare-winners/) when certain the trailing candidates no longer have a path to victory. ## About Prop 39 and other California ballot measures
Voter ID is actually on the November ballot.
Prop 39 is a ballot measure that, if approved by voters, would require voters to show a driver's license or other government ID to vote.
Supporters say it would tighter election rules through verified citizenship.
Opponents say it would make it harder for Californians to vote.
...

California law allows county elections officials up to 30 days to complete the official canvass and processed.
Updated election results will be provided by NBCLA and Telemundo 52.

Voting by mail?
You'd write the last four digits of an ID number — your driver's license, for example — on the return envelope.
Don't have an ID?
The state would be required to give you a free voter ID card, no charge, if you ask for one.

How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

All Haley breaks loose
By MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason), BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones) and JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white)
11/02/2026 09:00 AM EST
Voting stickers | David Swanson/AFP via Getty Images
DRIVING THE DAY — Gavin Newsom redoubled his support for Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed , after his rival in the primary, Haley Stevens , made a shock endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday morning.
But Newsom’s response — a post on X (https://x.com/GavinNewsom/status/2116963882321547624?a=a81hx_WxO-5-yTzeKvQ&s=20) affirming his support for El-Sayed without mentioning Stevens — was notably less lacerating than other Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , who said Stevens committed a “despicable betrayal.”
Appearing on the YouTube show 2Way (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ppJFvSvw5yY), Newsom was asked by conservative co-host Larry O’Connor whether Democrats were being hypocritical after years of urging Republicans to choose country over party and break with Trump.
“I don’t know enough about what ultimately led her to make that decision outside of what she said in that video. And she certainly has the right to do that, and I don’t condemn her on that basis. I don’t agree with her, and made that point clear,” Newsom said.
That was not sufficient for frequent Newsom antagonist Rep. Ro Khanna , who posted on X (https://x.com/RoKhanna/status/2117066889553650073?a=eHCTLwwsrEUVOUhEhso&s=20) linking the lack of condemnation to Newsom’s opposition to the billionaires tax, adding Newsom’s “Big Tent is just standing for nothing.”
Meanwhile, Kamala Harris recorded robo-calls supporting El-Sayed in Michigan. She did not make a public comment about Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers.
BEYOND THE TOPLINE — The California governor’s race sits at the top of the ticket, but Xavier Becerra vs. Steve Hilton isn’t where the drama is. That’s down the ballot.
These are the races that POLITICO California reporters will be refreshing on election night. Among them are a ballot measure that tests just how much voters want to stick it to billionaires, the Democratic incumbents who may be swept out by demands for generational change, and a pair of contests in Los Angeles that could establish democratic socialist dominance in the nation’s second largest city.
Here are our picks of the top races to watch.
Melanie Mason: Yes, the Los Angeles mayor’s race is the marquee contest in the city (more on that below). But don’t sleep on the little-watched city attorney’s race, where Marissa Roy , a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, appears poised to defeat (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-28/marissa-roys-lead-grows-over-john-mckinney-in-la-city-attorney-race) John McKinney , a centrist Democrat running on a law-and-order platform. While Nithya Raman ’s relationship with DSA has been fraught, Roy’s race has been a top priority for the group. If both Raman and Roy win their races, it would mean candidates from the insurgent left will occupy all three citywide offices (controller Kenneth Mejia , also a progressive, already won reelection outright in June with a commanding 63% of the vote). The prospect of a total progressive takeover in the country’s second-largest city would be a major flex for the ascendant DSA — and would make Los Angeles the leading laboratory of progressive governance.
Jeremy B. White: I’ll cheat a bit and say I’m curious to see the fate of three Democratic incumbents facing viable, well-funded Democratic challenges for safe seats: Rep. Doris Matsui in Sacramento, Rep. Mike Thompson in northern California and Rep. Jimmy Gomez in Los Angeles. So much of the focus has deservedly been on whether Democrats win the reconfigured Prop 50 districts to secure a majority. But at a time of generational turnover and roiling anti-establishment discontent — plus a dose of scandal (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/19/jimmy-gomez-house-ethics-sexual-misconduct-staffer-01041651), in Gomez’s case — blue seats could flip, too. Democrats will likely reclaim the House. But it’s less clear what they’d do with power — and that’s largely because of the kind of internal divisions on display in these races.
Blake Jones: Moderate Democrat Adam Gray and progressive populist Randy Villegas , who are both running in competitive districts in the Central Valley, could tell us a lot (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/09/how-to-win-the-central-valley-01113264) about how the Democratic coalition is moving. Each should perform better than Democrats did in their respective regions in 2024, given the atmosphere we’re in. But if Gray or Villegas does so by a noticeably larger margin, that would be a signal that their brand of politics is faring better in the Valley, and likely, among their districts’ Latino voter majorities. If they perform similarly — or if Gray only gets a slight edge from his incumbency advantage — that would be a sign that voters are simply moving away from Republicans and not toward a specific kind of Democratic message.
Will McCarthy: It has been 15 years since Occupy Wall Street brought the issue of wealth inequality to the center of political discourse in the United States. Billionaires and their bottomless resources had a growing influence over the political system, and the concept of the 1% and the 99% became a familiar part of the American political lexicon.
But years later, through three presidential campaigns and countless Bernie Sanders speeches, voters until now have never had the chance to weigh in on the issue in such a direct way as Proposition 40, a one-time tax on California’s billionaires. The issue pits a fractured coalition against an opponent with endless resources, and the polling suggests the measure is running behind. But will voters, who routinely express a dour view of billionaires (https://www.dataforprogress.org/blog/2026/8/13/voters-think-billionaires-earned-their-wealth-through-exploitation-not-hard-work), vote to pass the measure simply to stick it to the man?
Daniel Miller: Los Angeles’ mayoral race is a strange brew of grievance and policy. Incumbent Karen Bass and Councilmember Nithya Raman , once allies, are now skirmishing over homelessness, housing affordability and how to best prepare for the 2028 Olympics. The race has tightened (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/29/karen-bass-is-back-in-the-race-01140222), despite polls showing deep dissatisfaction with the mayor.
Raman, who narrowly bested Spencer Pratt in the primary, has criticized Bass’ homelessness strategy and her plan to loosen short-term-rental rules (https://www.thesportsexaminer.com/los-angeles-2028-l-a-mayor-bass-proposing-rule-change-to-allow-more-airbnb-rentals-in-2028-motions-on-la28-purchases-reimbursements-headed-to-council/) during the Games. Hollywood is another fault line: Raman vows to bring production jobs back, though she recused herself from four of seven council votes (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/23/nithya-ramans-answer-to-the-hollywood-question-01133465) on entertainment industry-related measures because her husband works in television. The winner will help lead both the city’s Olympic preparations and its response to Hollywood’s jobs crisis, which has been fomented by years of runaway production (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/08/16/hollywood-film-production-illinois-tax-credits-01037735?utm_medium=activitypub). A Raman victory would mark a sea change at City Hall and thrust her into the national spotlight, inviting comparisons to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani — whether or not they hold up (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/02/09/new-mayoral-challenger-in-los-angeles-draws-mamdani-comparisons-00771033) under close examination.
Liam Dillon: Lots of people are talking about the LA mayor’s race and I’ll add to the chorus, but through the lens of housing. A Raman win combined with the expected victory of Janeese Lewis George as mayor of Washington D.C., would be a boon to the burgeoning nationwide “Left-YIMBY (https://x.com/Janeese4DC/status/2109410845113618690)” movement. Raman, Lewis George and Mamdani all are members of the Democratic Socialists of America and promise to expand protections for tenants as part of their agendas. But at the same time, they’ve embraced the role of the private market in housing development and have pledged to remove zoning restrictions and other municipal barriers to growth — policies favored by pro-growth, Yes In My Backyard activists.
As I’ve written, the idea faces healthy skepticism (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/03/07/mamdani-nithya-raman-housing-socialism-abundance-00817314). One centrist critic calls Left-YIMBYism “capitalism for developers, communism for landlords.” But its supporters believe its potential success could end the left’s housing wars and lead to an enduring, renter-centered political coalition.
Tyler Katzenberger: Will tech’s spending spree in state legislative races pay off? A North Bay Assembly contest between fellow Democrats Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward offers a test: Grow California, funded by crypto executives Chris Larsen and Tim Draper , has cumulatively spent more than $1 million backing Lucan and opposing Elward, labor’s favored candidate. A Lucan win would help validate the industry’s strategy of swaying state politics by spending big in Dem-on-Dem races, while an Elward victory would be a triumph for labor leaders who increasingly find themselves at war with tech interests.
The race also has high stakes for Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas , who ruffled feathers among the Legislature’s Black and Progressive caucuses (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/11/rivas-assembly-senate-endorsements-01144382) by endorsing Lucan, who is seen as the more moderate candidate, over Elward, a Black woman and self-identified progressive.
Lindsey Holden: Proposition 39, California’s voter ID ballot measure, once looked like it might have a real shot. Polling earlier this year suggested the concept was broadly popular (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2026/05/04/california-democrats-voter-id-00905425), and Democrats were slow to mount an opposition campaign (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/04/californias-fight-against-voter-id-is-a-slow-burn-00905656). But in the months since the primary, voting rights groups, labor, legislative leaders, Gov. Gavin Newsom and his likely successor, Xavier Becerra , all lined up against it (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/24/california-dems-ramp-up-anti-voter-id-fight-01011990), relentlessly yoking the measure to Trump.
The messaging seems to have paid off. The measure is trailing in polls (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/california-voter-id-measure-falling-short-in-new-poll-01127047), and the president’s ongoing efforts to exert control over California’s elections (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2026/10/15/california-noncitizen-voting-lawsuit-01121542) likely isn’t helping Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio create the bipartisan coalition he would have needed to make it law.
Saqib Rahim: The traditionally low-profile race for insurance commissioner has become a dramatic faceoff this year between an up-and-coming progressive, former Sanders campaigner Jane Kim , and an experienced Sacramento Democrat, state Sen. Ben Allen , whose own mom was displaced by the LA fires. On its face, it’s a classic insider-outsider battle. But it’s also become a debate about government: how extensively the government should intervene when people feel crushed by the cost of living, versus trusting market forces to fix things. It’s a debate Republicans and Democrats are having around America about an issue that is only going to become more urgent on a hotter planet.
Alex Nieves: A handful of Assembly races could help progressives gain ground in a chamber dominated by moderates in recent years. That includes the Orange County district where Sanders-backed candidate Jessie Lopez is challenging fellow Democrat David Penaloza . Lopez, a Santa Ana City Council member and member of the Working Families Party, has garnered endorsements from progressives like Assemblymember Alex Lee and state Sen. Caroline Menjivar , while Penaloza has the support of Rivas and the California Democratic Party. The oil industry has also come out against Lopez, contributing to an independent expenditure committee that’s spent more than $1 million to oppose her.

If both Raman and Roy win their races, it would mean candidates from the insurgent left will occupy all three citywide offices (controller Kenneth Mejia , also a progressive, already won reelection outright in June with a commanding 63% of the vote). The prospect of a total progressive takeover in the country’s second-largest city would be a major flex for the ascendant DSA — and would make Los Angeles the leading laboratory of progressive governance.

Doris Matsui in Sacramento, Rep. Mike Thompson in northern California and Rep. Jimmy Gomez in Los Angeles. So much of the focus has deservedly been on whether Democrats win the reconfigured Prop 50 districts to secure a majority. If they perform similarly — or if Gray only gets a slight edge from his incumbency advantage — that would be a sign that voters are simply moving away from Republicans and not toward a specific kind of Democratic message.

Billionaires and their bottomless resources had a growing influence over the political system, and the concept of the 1% and the 99% became a familiar part of the American political lexicon.

Incumbent Karen Bass and Councilmember Nithya Raman , once allies, are now skirmishing over homelessness, housing affordability and how to best prepare for the 2028 Olympics. The race has tightened (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/29/karen-bass-is-back-in-the-race-01140222), despite polls showing deep dissatisfaction with the mayor.

Hollywood is another fault line: Raman vows to bring production jobs back, though she recused herself from four of seven council votes (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/23/nithya-ramans-answer-to-the-hollywood-question-01133465) on entertainment industry-related measures because her husband works in television. The winner will help lead both the city’s Olympic preparations and its response to Hollywood’s jobs crisis, which has been fomented by years of runaway production (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/08/16/hollywood-film-production-illinois-tax-credits-01037735?utm_medium=activitypub). A Raman victory would mark a sea change at City Hall and thrust her into the national spotlight, inviting comparisons to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani — whether or not they hold up (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/02/09/new-mayoral-challenger-in-los-angeles-draws-mamdani-comparisons-00771033) under close examination.

A Raman win combined with the expected victory of Janeese Lewis George as mayor of Washington D.C., would be a boon to the burgeoning nationwide “Left-YIMBY (https://x.com/Janeese4DC/status/2109410845113618690)” movement. Raman, Lewis George and Mamdani all are members of the Democratic Socialists of America and promise to expand protections for tenants as part of their agendas. But at the same time, they’ve embraced the role of the private market in housing development and have pledged to remove zoning restrictions and other municipal barriers to growth — policies favored by pro-growth, Yes In My Backyard activists.

By MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason), BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones) and JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white)

DRIVING THE DAY — Gavin Newsom redoubled his support for Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed , after his rival in the primary, Haley Stevens , made a shock endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday morning.
But Newsom’s response — a post on X (https://x.com/GavinNewsom/status/2116963882321547624?a=a81hx_WxO-5-yTzeKvQ&s=20) affirming his support for El-Sayed without mentioning Stevens — was notably less lacerating than other Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , who said Stevens committed a “despicable betrayal.”
Appearing on the YouTube show 2Way (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ppJFvSvw5yY), Newsom was asked by conservative co-host Larry O’Connor whether Democrats were being hypocritical after years of urging Republicans to choose country over party and break with Trump.
“I don’t know enough about what ultimately led her to make that decision outside of what she said in that video. And she certainly has the right to do that, and I don’t condemn her on that basis. I don’t agree with her, and made that point clear,” Newsom said.
That was not sufficient for frequent Newsom antagonist Rep. Ro Khanna , who posted on X (https://x.com/RoKhanna/status/2117066889553650073?a=eHCTLwwsrEUVOUhEhso&s=20) linking the lack of condemnation to Newsom’s opposition to the billionaires tax, adding Newsom’s “Big Tent is just standing for nothing.”
Meanwhile, Kamala Harris recorded robo-calls supporting El-Sayed in Michigan. She did not make a public comment about Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers.

All Haley breaks loose
By MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason), BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones) and JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white)
11/02/2026 09:00 AM EST
Voting stickers | David Swanson/AFP via Getty Images
DRIVING THE DAY — Gavin Newsom redoubled his support for Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed , after his rival in the primary, Haley Stevens , made a shock endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday morning.
But Newsom’s response — a post on X (https://x.com/GavinNewsom/status/2116963882321547624?a=a81hx_WxO-5-yTzeKvQ&s=20) affirming his support for El-Sayed without mentioning Stevens — was notably less lacerating than other Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , who said Stevens committed a “despicable betrayal.”
Appearing on the YouTube show 2Way (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ppJFvSvw5yY), Newsom was asked by conservative co-host Larry O’Connor whether Democrats were being hypocritical after years of urging Republicans to choose country over party and break with Trump.
“I don’t know enough about what ultimately led her to make that decision outside of what she said in that video. And she certainly has the right to do that, and I don’t condemn her on that basis. I don’t agree with her, and made that point clear,” Newsom said.
That was not sufficient for frequent Newsom antagonist Rep. Ro Khanna , who posted on X (https://x.com/RoKhanna/status/2117066889553650073?a=eHCTLwwsrEUVOUhEhso&s=20) linking the lack of condemnation to Newsom’s opposition to the billionaires tax, adding Newsom’s “Big Tent is just standing for nothing.”
Meanwhile, Kamala Harris recorded robo-calls supporting El-Sayed in Michigan. She did not make a public comment about Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers.
BEYOND THE TOPLINE — The California governor’s race sits at the top of the ticket, but Xavier Becerra vs. Steve Hilton isn’t where the drama is. That’s down the ballot.
These are the races that POLITICO California reporters will be refreshing on election night. Among them are a ballot measure that tests just how much voters want to stick it to billionaires, the Democratic incumbents who may be swept out by demands for generational change, and a pair of contests in Los Angeles that could establish democratic socialist dominance in the nation’s second largest city.
Here are our picks of the top races to watch.
Melanie Mason: Yes, the Los Angeles mayor’s race is the marquee contest in the city (more on that below). But don’t sleep on the little-watched city attorney’s race, where Marissa Roy , a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, appears poised to defeat (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-28/marissa-roys-lead-grows-over-john-mckinney-in-la-city-attorney-race) John McKinney , a centrist Democrat running on a law-and-order platform. While Nithya Raman ’s relationship with DSA has been fraught, Roy’s race has been a top priority for the group. If both Raman and Roy win their races, it would mean candidates from the insurgent left will occupy all three citywide offices (controller Kenneth Mejia , also a progressive, already won reelection outright in June with a commanding 63% of the vote). The prospect of a total progressive takeover in the country’s second-largest city would be a major flex for the ascendant DSA — and would make Los Angeles the leading laboratory of progressive governance.
Jeremy B. White: I’ll cheat a bit and say I’m curious to see the fate of three Democratic incumbents facing viable, well-funded Democratic challenges for safe seats: Rep. Doris Matsui in Sacramento, Rep. Mike Thompson in northern California and Rep. Jimmy Gomez in Los Angeles. So much of the focus has deservedly been on whether Democrats win the reconfigured Prop 50 districts to secure a majority. But at a time of generational turnover and roiling anti-establishment discontent — plus a dose of scandal (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/19/jimmy-gomez-house-ethics-sexual-misconduct-staffer-01041651), in Gomez’s case — blue seats could flip, too. Democrats will likely reclaim the House. But it’s less clear what they’d do with power — and that’s largely because of the kind of internal divisions on display in these races.
Blake Jones: Moderate Democrat Adam Gray and progressive populist Randy Villegas , who are both running in competitive districts in the Central Valley, could tell us a lot (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/09/how-to-win-the-central-valley-01113264) about how the Democratic coalition is moving. Each should perform better than Democrats did in their respective regions in 2024, given the atmosphere we’re in. But if Gray or Villegas does so by a noticeably larger margin, that would be a signal that their brand of politics is faring better in the Valley, and likely, among their districts’ Latino voter majorities. If they perform similarly — or if Gray only gets a slight edge from his incumbency advantage — that would be a sign that voters are simply moving away from Republicans and not toward a specific kind of Democratic message.
Will McCarthy: It has been 15 years since Occupy Wall Street brought the issue of wealth inequality to the center of political discourse in the United States. Billionaires and their bottomless resources had a growing influence over the political system, and the concept of the 1% and the 99% became a familiar part of the American political lexicon.
But years later, through three presidential campaigns and countless Bernie Sanders speeches, voters until now have never had the chance to weigh in on the issue in such a direct way as Proposition 40, a one-time tax on California’s billionaires. The issue pits a fractured coalition against an opponent with endless resources, and the polling suggests the measure is running behind. But will voters, who routinely express a dour view of billionaires (https://www.dataforprogress.org/blog/2026/8/13/voters-think-billionaires-earned-their-wealth-through-exploitation-not-hard-work), vote to pass the measure simply to stick it to the man?
Daniel Miller: Los Angeles’ mayoral race is a strange brew of grievance and policy. Incumbent Karen Bass and Councilmember Nithya Raman , once allies, are now skirmishing over homelessness, housing affordability and how to best prepare for the 2028 Olympics. The race has tightened (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/29/karen-bass-is-back-in-the-race-01140222), despite polls showing deep dissatisfaction with the mayor.
Raman, who narrowly bested Spencer Pratt in the primary, has criticized Bass’ homelessness strategy and her plan to loosen short-term-rental rules (https://www.thesportsexaminer.com/los-angeles-2028-l-a-mayor-bass-proposing-rule-change-to-allow-more-airbnb-rentals-in-2028-motions-on-la28-purchases-reimbursements-headed-to-council/) during the Games. Hollywood is another fault line: Raman vows to bring production jobs back, though she recused herself from four of seven council votes (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/23/nithya-ramans-answer-to-the-hollywood-question-01133465) on entertainment industry-related measures because her husband works in television. The winner will help lead both the city’s Olympic preparations and its response to Hollywood’s jobs crisis, which has been fomented by years of runaway production (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/08/16/hollywood-film-production-illinois-tax-credits-01037735?utm_medium=activitypub). A Raman victory would mark a sea change at City Hall and thrust her into the national spotlight, inviting comparisons to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani — whether or not they hold up (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/02/09/new-mayoral-challenger-in-los-angeles-draws-mamdani-comparisons-00771033) under close examination.
Liam Dillon: Lots of people are talking about the LA mayor’s race and I’ll add to the chorus, but through the lens of housing. A Raman win combined with the expected victory of Janeese Lewis George as mayor of Washington D.C., would be a boon to the burgeoning nationwide “Left-YIMBY (https://x.com/Janeese4DC/status/2109410845113618690)” movement. Raman, Lewis George and Mamdani all are members of the Democratic Socialists of America and promise to expand protections for tenants as part of their agendas. But at the same time, they’ve embraced the role of the private market in housing development and have pledged to remove zoning restrictions and other municipal barriers to growth — policies favored by pro-growth, Yes In My Backyard activists.
As I’ve written, the idea faces healthy skepticism (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/03/07/mamdani-nithya-raman-housing-socialism-abundance-00817314). One centrist critic calls Left-YIMBYism “capitalism for developers, communism for landlords.” But its supporters believe its potential success could end the left’s housing wars and lead to an enduring, renter-centered political coalition.
Tyler Katzenberger: Will tech’s spending spree in state legislative races pay off? A North Bay Assembly contest between fellow Democrats Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward offers a test: Grow California, funded by crypto executives Chris Larsen and Tim Draper , has cumulatively spent more than $1 million backing Lucan and opposing Elward, labor’s favored candidate. A Lucan win would help validate the industry’s strategy of swaying state politics by spending big in Dem-on-Dem races, while an Elward victory would be a triumph for labor leaders who increasingly find themselves at war with tech interests.
The race also has high stakes for Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas , who ruffled feathers among the Legislature’s Black and Progressive caucuses (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/11/rivas-assembly-senate-endorsements-01144382) by endorsing Lucan, who is seen as the more moderate candidate, over Elward, a Black woman and self-identified progressive.
Lindsey Holden: Proposition 39, California’s voter ID ballot measure, once looked like it might have a real shot. Polling earlier this year suggested the concept was broadly popular (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2026/05/04/california-democrats-voter-id-00905425), and Democrats were slow to mount an opposition campaign (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/04/californias-fight-against-voter-id-is-a-slow-burn-00905656). But in the months since the primary, voting rights groups, labor, legislative leaders, Gov. Gavin Newsom and his likely successor, Xavier Becerra , all lined up against it (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/24/california-dems-ramp-up-anti-voter-id-fight-01011990), relentlessly yoking the measure to Trump.
The messaging seems to have paid off. The measure is trailing in polls (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/california-voter-id-measure-falling-short-in-new-poll-01127047), and the president’s ongoing efforts to exert control over California’s elections (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2026/10/15/california-noncitizen-voting-lawsuit-01121542) likely isn’t helping Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio create the bipartisan coalition he would have needed to make it law.
Saqib Rahim: The traditionally low-profile race for insurance commissioner has become a dramatic faceoff this year between an up-and-coming progressive, former Sanders campaigner Jane Kim , and an experienced Sacramento Democrat, state Sen. Ben Allen , whose own mom was displaced by the LA fires. On its face, it’s a classic insider-outsider battle. But it’s also become a debate about government: how extensively the government should intervene when people feel crushed by the cost of living, versus trusting market forces to fix things. It’s a debate Republicans and Democrats are having around America about an issue that is only going to become more urgent on a hotter planet.
Alex Nieves: A handful of Assembly races could help progressives gain ground in a chamber dominated by moderates in recent years. That includes the Orange County district where Sanders-backed candidate Jessie Lopez is challenging fellow Democrat David Penaloza . Lopez, a Santa Ana City Council member and member of the Working Families Party, has garnered endorsements from progressives like Assemblymember Alex Lee and state Sen. Caroline Menjivar , while Penaloza has the support of Rivas and the California Democratic Party. The oil industry has also come out against Lopez, contributing to an independent expenditure committee that’s spent more than $1 million to oppose her.

https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/elections/california-proposition-39-voter-id-measure-divides-democrats-and-republicans/103-9189352d-c2d8-4bbb-a54c-000de59f6619
SACRAMENTO, Calif.
— With Election Day approaching, California voters are weighing Proposition 39, a voter ID initiative that has drawn opposition from prominent Democrats and support from Republicans.
If passed by voters, the measure would require voters to present government-issued identification at polling places.
Voters casting ballots by mail would have to write the last four digits of a government-issued ID on the return envelope.
More in Politics
The proposal would also create a free, state-issued voter ID card for voters who request one and require more routine maintenance of voter registration rolls.
The California Democratic Party, including Governor Gavin Newsom and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra, opposes the measure, arguing it could make voting more difficult for eligible voters.
At a No on Prop.
39 event in San Francisco's Japantown on Tuesday, opponents displayed signs in five languages urging voters to reject Proposition 39.
'This is California.
We can do better,' said Jodi Hicks, one of the opponents, and CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California.
Johanna Liu, president and CEO of the San Francisco Community Clinic Consortium, said the measure could disproportionately affect people with fewer resources.
...
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican and proponent of the measure, said it would preserve mail-in voting while establishing a straightforward identification requirement.

2. EDITORIAL: We asked the No on Prop. 39 campaign why voters should reject the measure
https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-39-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/
Californians are being asked to vote "yes" or "no" on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office, would require election officials to verify Californians' U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID.
It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting "yes" would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you're voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting "no" means the process stays is it is - you don't need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans' currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump's unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters.
It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.

# Judge rejects challenge to California attorney general’s description of voter ID measure
A state judge Thursday rejected a challenge to how California Atty.
Gen. Rob Bonta’s office summarized a strict new voter ID measure on November ballots — ruling that the summary language accurately describes the measure’s effects were it to pass.
Another judge dealt the backers of the measure a second loss by tentatively finding that their description of the measure, submitted for the official state voter’s guide, was misleading.
They had claimed that Proposition 39 would make voting easier.
In the first case, Sacramento County Superior Court Judge Jennifer K. Rockwell ruled that the label, title and summary of the certified ballot measure accurately describe Proposition 39 as a measure that “prohibits citizens from voting” — language the measure’s backers specifically objected to — unless they provide a government-issued ID.
According to minutes from a Thursday hearing on the matter, Rockwell concluded that, to the extent the measure’s backers object to that language, they are objecting to “the provisions of the measure itself.”
Rockwell rejected the argument put forth by the measure’s backers that it would not prevent people without ID from voting, only their votes from being counted — a distinction the judge found lacking.

https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/elections/california-proposition-39-voter-id-measure-divides-democrats-and-republicans/103-9189352d-c2d8-4bbb-a54c-000de59f6619
SACRAMENTO, Calif.
— With Election Day approaching, California voters are weighing Proposition 39, a voter ID initiative that has drawn opposition from prominent Democrats and support from Republicans.
If passed by voters, the measure would require voters to present government-issued identification at polling places.
Voters casting ballots by mail would have to write the last four digits of a government-issued ID on the return envelope.
More in Politics
The proposal would also create a free, state-issued voter ID card for voters who request one and require more routine maintenance of voter registration rolls.
The California Democratic Party, including Governor Gavin Newsom and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra, opposes the measure, arguing it could make voting more difficult for eligible voters.
At a No on Prop.
39 event in San Francisco's Japantown on Tuesday, opponents displayed signs in five languages urging voters to reject Proposition 39.
'This is California.
We can do better,' said Jodi Hicks, one of the opponents, and CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California.
Johanna Liu, president and CEO of the San Francisco Community Clinic Consortium, said the measure could disproportionately affect people with fewer resources.
...

2. EDITORIAL: We asked the No on Prop. 39 campaign why voters should reject the measure
https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-39-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/
Californians are being asked to vote "yes" or "no" on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office, would require election officials to verify Californians' U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID.
It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting "yes" would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you're voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting "no" means the process stays is it is - you don't need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans' currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump's unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters.
It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.

# Judge rejects challenge to California attorney general’s description of voter ID measure
A state judge Thursday rejected a challenge to how California Atty.
Gen. Rob Bonta’s office summarized a strict new voter ID measure on November ballots — ruling that the summary language accurately describes the measure’s effects were it to pass.
Another judge dealt the backers of the measure a second loss by tentatively finding that their description of the measure, submitted for the official state voter’s guide, was misleading.
They had claimed that Proposition 39 would make voting easier.
In the first case, Sacramento County Superior Court Judge Jennifer K. Rockwell ruled that the label, title and summary of the certified ballot measure accurately describe Proposition 39 as a measure that “prohibits citizens from voting” — language the measure’s backers specifically objected to — unless they provide a government-issued ID.
According to minutes from a Thursday hearing on the matter, Rockwell concluded that, to the extent the measure’s backers object to that language, they are objecting to “the provisions of the measure itself.”
Rockwell rejected the argument put forth by the measure’s backers that it would not prevent people without ID from voting, only their votes from being counted — a distinction the judge found lacking.

I haven't found any results yet, since the election on November 3, 2026 is still upcoming. I'll check the LA Times report on the IGS poll from October 29 and the PPIC October survey too. I also want to think through why the polls could be off, since voter ID measures have passed in other states like Nevada, but California's situation is quite different.

I'm comparing this to California's 2024 Prop 36, which passed with about 68% even though Newsom opposed it, so California voters can back conservative measures. A voter ID measure is much more partisan, though, and it lands in a midterm with Trump in office and Democrats energized, plus Prop 50 passed with about 64% in November 2025. I'll also check the LA Times IGS article for the exact question wording and whether undecided voters lean one way.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires’ assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.

Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Mark DiCamillo, the poll’s director, said previous surveys showed support for Proposition 40 has been fragile, and the most recent shows its prospects have dimmed as election day approaches.
The increase in opposition to Proposition 40 is “broad-based and spans virtually all major segments of the electorate,” DiCamillio said. The ballot measure was leading in a Berkeley poll conducted just six weeks ago, albeit by a slim margin, so its reversal of fortune is significant, he said.
Advertisement
The declining support comes after an onslaught of money spent opposing Proposition 40, including a torrent of television and social media ads airing everywhere from NFL games to “Everybody Loves Raymond” reruns. Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of billionaires who resided in California as of Jan. 1, with some exceptions. Democrats and their allies are splintered over the proposal. Some, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argue it will prompt the wealthy to flee California, further harming its volatile budget, which is dependent on the state’s richest residents. The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll.
The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California’s richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”
He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.

I haven't found any results yet, since the election on November 3, 2026 is still upcoming. I'll check the LA Times report on the IGS poll from October 29 and the PPIC October survey too. I also want to think through why the polls could be off, since voter ID measures have passed in other states like Nevada, but California's situation is quite different.

I'm comparing this to California's 2024 Prop 36, which passed with about 68% even though Newsom opposed it, so California voters can back conservative measures. A voter ID measure is much more partisan, though, and it lands in a midterm with Trump in office and Democrats energized, plus Prop 50 passed with about 64% in November 2025. I'll also check the LA Times IGS article for the exact question wording and whether undecided voters lean one way.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires’ assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Mark DiCamillo, the poll’s director, said previous surveys showed support for Proposition 40 has been fragile, and the most recent shows its prospects have dimmed as election day approaches.
The increase in opposition to Proposition 40 is “broad-based and spans virtually all major segments of the electorate,” DiCamillio said. The ballot measure was leading in a Berkeley poll conducted just six weeks ago, albeit by a slim margin, so its reversal of fortune is significant, he said.
Advertisement
The declining support comes after an onslaught of money spent opposing Proposition 40, including a torrent of television and social media ads airing everywhere from NFL games to “Everybody Loves Raymond” reruns. Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of billionaires who resided in California as of Jan. 1, with some exceptions. Democrats and their allies are splintered over the proposal. Some, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argue it will prompt the wealthy to flee California, further harming its volatile budget, which is dependent on the state’s richest residents. The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll.
The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California’s richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”
He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.

No results are in yet, since the election hasn't concluded and it's around November 2-3, 2026. The polling so far has most nonpartisan surveys showing the measure losing by wide margins, and even Republican-aligned pollsters show it trailing.

I'm also weighing whether a SurveyUSA result showing it ahead might have used different wording, though that doesn't change the overall picture.

No results are in yet, since the election hasn't concluded and it's around November 2-3, 2026. The polling so far has most nonpartisan surveys showing the measure losing by wide margins, and even Republican-aligned pollsters show it trailing.

I'm going through the remaining polls, where a few show Prop 39 narrowly ahead but none above 50%. I'm also noting that DeMaio's internal poll had it down 4, prediction markets put passage around 13-15%, and the ballot title reads unfavorably. The political climate and major opposition from state leaders and labor point toward No.

I'm running the numbers on partisan composition: with Democrats around half the electorate and Republicans near 29%, a Yes share in the mid-40s seems likely, so the measure would still fall short. I'm also weighing whether a SurveyUSA result showing it ahead might have used different wording, though that doesn't change the overall picture.

***Requires Voters to Select Government-Issued Identification for Voting by Mail.*** Proposition 39 requires new and existing voters to select a government-issued identification in their voter registration to vote by mail.
***Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote.*** Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California.
Elections officials would be required to verify voters’ identities before counting their ballots.
The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail:
- ***In-Person Voting.*** When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.
- ***Voting by Mail.*** When voting by mail, Proposition 39 requires voters to provide the last four digits of their selected government-issued identification number on the ballot envelope.
Elections officials would verify that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information.

the nation waits for results, who do you trust? For 178 years, AP has been the steady voice America turns to on election night. Our reporters, election analysts and graphics journalists simply tell you who won — no spin, no bias, just facts. We're not owned by billionaires. We don't have an editorial agenda. We just count votes and report results, the same way we've done since 1848. Democracy itself depends on having one trusted source that puts facts above everything else. DONATE (https://apnews.com/donate?target=election_results) About AP’s election results and race calls The Associated Press (https://www.ap.org/elections/our-role/) first tabulated vote counts in U.S. elections in 1848 and today gathers election results (https://www.ap.org/elections/our-role-in-the-u-s-elections/how-ap-counts-the-vote/) from local election officials in thousands of races nationwide. Results are reported as soon as they are available. AP’s Decision Team declares winners (https://www.ap.org/elections/our-role-in-the-u-s-elections/how-we-declare-winners/) when certain the trailing candidates no longer have a path to victory. California voters decide 14 statewide propositions on November 3, 2026. On Kalshi and Polymarket, traders buy contracts on whether each one passes, and a contract’s price is the market’s chance. This page puts every measure side by side, with each venue’s price, and updates through the day.
For the separate statewide candidate contest on the same ballot, compare the California governor election (https://defirate.com/odds/california-governor/). For national races on the same election calendar, compare 2026 congressional midterm odds (https://defirate.com/odds/2026-midterms/); these proposition markets settle separate ballot questions.
How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

All Haley breaks loose
By MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason), BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones) and JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white)
11/02/2026 09:00 AM EST
Voting stickers | David Swanson/AFP via Getty Images
DRIVING THE DAY — Gavin Newsom redoubled his support for Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed , after his rival in the primary, Haley Stevens , made a shock endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday morning.
But Newsom’s response — a post on X (https://x.com/GavinNewsom/status/2116963882321547624?a=a81hx_WxO-5-yTzeKvQ&s=20) affirming his support for El-Sayed without mentioning Stevens — was notably less lacerating than other Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , who said Stevens committed a “despicable betrayal.”
Appearing on the YouTube show 2Way (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ppJFvSvw5yY), Newsom was asked by conservative co-host Larry O’Connor whether Democrats were being hypocritical after years of urging Republicans to choose country over party and break with Trump.
“I don’t know enough about what ultimately led her to make that decision outside of what she said in that video. And she certainly has the right to do that, and I don’t condemn her on that basis. I don’t agree with her, and made that point clear,” Newsom said.
That was not sufficient for frequent Newsom antagonist Rep. Ro Khanna , who posted on X (https://x.com/RoKhanna/status/2117066889553650073?a=eHCTLwwsrEUVOUhEhso&s=20) linking the lack of condemnation to Newsom’s opposition to the billionaires tax, adding Newsom’s “Big Tent is just standing for nothing.”
Meanwhile, Kamala Harris recorded robo-calls supporting El-Sayed in Michigan. She did not make a public comment about Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers.
BEYOND THE TOPLINE — The California governor’s race sits at the top of the ticket, but Xavier Becerra vs. Steve Hilton isn’t where the drama is. That’s down the ballot.
These are the races that POLITICO California reporters will be refreshing on election night. Among them are a ballot measure that tests just how much voters want to stick it to billionaires, the Democratic incumbents who may be swept out by demands for generational change, and a pair of contests in Los Angeles that could establish democratic socialist dominance in the nation’s second largest city.
Here are our picks of the top races to watch.
Melanie Mason: Yes, the Los Angeles mayor’s race is the marquee contest in the city (more on that below). But don’t sleep on the little-watched city attorney’s race, where Marissa Roy , a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, appears poised to defeat (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-28/marissa-roys-lead-grows-over-john-mckinney-in-la-city-attorney-race) John McKinney , a centrist Democrat running on a law-and-order platform. While Nithya Raman ’s relationship with DSA has been fraught, Roy’s race has been a top priority for the group. If both Raman and Roy win their races, it would mean candidates from the insurgent left will occupy all three citywide offices (controller Kenneth Mejia , also a progressive, already won reelection outright in June with a commanding 63% of the vote). The prospect of a total progressive takeover in the country’s second-largest city would be a major flex for the ascendant DSA — and would make Los Angeles the leading laboratory of progressive governance.
Jeremy B. White: I’ll cheat a bit and say I’m curious to see the fate of three Democratic incumbents facing viable, well-funded Democratic challenges for safe seats: Rep. Doris Matsui in Sacramento, Rep. Mike Thompson in northern California and Rep. Jimmy Gomez in Los Angeles. So much of the focus has deservedly been on whether Democrats win the reconfigured Prop 50 districts to secure a majority. But at a time of generational turnover and roiling anti-establishment discontent — plus a dose of scandal (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/19/jimmy-gomez-house-ethics-sexual-misconduct-staffer-01041651), in Gomez’s case — blue seats could flip, too. Democrats will likely reclaim the House. But it’s less clear what they’d do with power — and that’s largely because of the kind of internal divisions on display in these races.
Blake Jones: Moderate Democrat Adam Gray and progressive populist Randy Villegas , who are both running in competitive districts in the Central Valley, could tell us a lot (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/09/how-to-win-the-central-valley-01113264) about how the Democratic coalition is moving. Each should perform better than Democrats did in their respective regions in 2024, given the atmosphere we’re in. But if Gray or Villegas does so by a noticeably larger margin, that would be a signal that their brand of politics is faring better in the Valley, and likely, among their districts’ Latino voter majorities. If they perform similarly — or if Gray only gets a slight edge from his incumbency advantage — that would be a sign that voters are simply moving away from Republicans and not toward a specific kind of Democratic message.
Will McCarthy: It has been 15 years since Occupy Wall Street brought the issue of wealth inequality to the center of political discourse in the United States. Billionaires and their bottomless resources had a growing influence over the political system, and the concept of the 1% and the 99% became a familiar part of the American political lexicon.
But years later, through three presidential campaigns and countless Bernie Sanders speeches, voters until now have never had the chance to weigh in on the issue in such a direct way as Proposition 40, a one-time tax on California’s billionaires. The issue pits a fractured coalition against an opponent with endless resources, and the polling suggests the measure is running behind. But will voters, who routinely express a dour view of billionaires (https://www.dataforprogress.org/blog/2026/8/13/voters-think-billionaires-earned-their-wealth-through-exploitation-not-hard-work), vote to pass the measure simply to stick it to the man?
Daniel Miller: Los Angeles’ mayoral race is a strange brew of grievance and policy. Incumbent Karen Bass and Councilmember Nithya Raman , once allies, are now skirmishing over homelessness, housing affordability and how to best prepare for the 2028 Olympics. The race has tightened (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/29/karen-bass-is-back-in-the-race-01140222), despite polls showing deep dissatisfaction with the mayor.
Raman, who narrowly bested Spencer Pratt in the primary, has criticized Bass’ homelessness strategy and her plan to loosen short-term-rental rules (https://www.thesportsexaminer.com/los-angeles-2028-l-a-mayor-bass-proposing-rule-change-to-allow-more-airbnb-rentals-in-2028-motions-on-la28-purchases-reimbursements-headed-to-council/) during the Games. Hollywood is another fault line: Raman vows to bring production jobs back, though she recused herself from four of seven council votes (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/23/nithya-ramans-answer-to-the-hollywood-question-01133465) on entertainment industry-related measures because her husband works in television. The winner will help lead both the city’s Olympic preparations and its response to Hollywood’s jobs crisis, which has been fomented by years of runaway production (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/08/16/hollywood-film-production-illinois-tax-credits-01037735?utm_medium=activitypub). A Raman victory would mark a sea change at City Hall and thrust her into the national spotlight, inviting comparisons to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani — whether or not they hold up (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/02/09/new-mayoral-challenger-in-los-angeles-draws-mamdani-comparisons-00771033) under close examination.
Liam Dillon: Lots of people are talking about the LA mayor’s race and I’ll add to the chorus, but through the lens of housing. A Raman win combined with the expected victory of Janeese Lewis George as mayor of Washington D.C., would be a boon to the burgeoning nationwide “Left-YIMBY (https://x.com/Janeese4DC/status/2109410845113618690)” movement. Raman, Lewis George and Mamdani all are members of the Democratic Socialists of America and promise to expand protections for tenants as part of their agendas. But at the same time, they’ve embraced the role of the private market in housing development and have pledged to remove zoning restrictions and other municipal barriers to growth — policies favored by pro-growth, Yes In My Backyard activists.
As I’ve written, the idea faces healthy skepticism (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/03/07/mamdani-nithya-raman-housing-socialism-abundance-00817314). One centrist critic calls Left-YIMBYism “capitalism for developers, communism for landlords.” But its supporters believe its potential success could end the left’s housing wars and lead to an enduring, renter-centered political coalition.
Tyler Katzenberger: Will tech’s spending spree in state legislative races pay off? A North Bay Assembly contest between fellow Democrats Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward offers a test: Grow California, funded by crypto executives Chris Larsen and Tim Draper , has cumulatively spent more than $1 million backing Lucan and opposing Elward, labor’s favored candidate. A Lucan win would help validate the industry’s strategy of swaying state politics by spending big in Dem-on-Dem races, while an Elward victory would be a triumph for labor leaders who increasingly find themselves at war with tech interests.
The race also has high stakes for Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas , who ruffled feathers among the Legislature’s Black and Progressive caucuses (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/11/rivas-assembly-senate-endorsements-01144382) by endorsing Lucan, who is seen as the more moderate candidate, over Elward, a Black woman and self-identified progressive.
Lindsey Holden: Proposition 39, California’s voter ID ballot measure, once looked like it might have a real shot. Polling earlier this year suggested the concept was broadly popular (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2026/05/04/california-democrats-voter-id-00905425), and Democrats were slow to mount an opposition campaign (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/04/californias-fight-against-voter-id-is-a-slow-burn-00905656). But in the months since the primary, voting rights groups, labor, legislative leaders, Gov. Gavin Newsom and his likely successor, Xavier Becerra , all lined up against it (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/24/california-dems-ramp-up-anti-voter-id-fight-01011990), relentlessly yoking the measure to Trump.
The messaging seems to have paid off. The measure is trailing in polls (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/california-voter-id-measure-falling-short-in-new-poll-01127047), and the president’s ongoing efforts to exert control over California’s elections (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2026/10/15/california-noncitizen-voting-lawsuit-01121542) likely isn’t helping Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio create the bipartisan coalition he would have needed to make it law.
Saqib Rahim: The traditionally low-profile race for insurance commissioner has become a dramatic faceoff this year between an up-and-coming progressive, former Sanders campaigner Jane Kim , and an experienced Sacramento Democrat, state Sen. Ben Allen , whose own mom was displaced by the LA fires. On its face, it’s a classic insider-outsider battle. But it’s also become a debate about government: how extensively the government should intervene when people feel crushed by the cost of living, versus trusting market forces to fix things. It’s a debate Republicans and Democrats are having around America about an issue that is only going to become more urgent on a hotter planet.
Alex Nieves: A handful of Assembly races could help progressives gain ground in a chamber dominated by moderates in recent years. That includes the Orange County district where Sanders-backed candidate Jessie Lopez is challenging fellow Democrat David Penaloza . Lopez, a Santa Ana City Council member and member of the Working Families Party, has garnered endorsements from progressives like Assemblymember Alex Lee and state Sen. Caroline Menjivar , while Penaloza has the support of Rivas and the California Democratic Party. The oil industry has also come out against Lopez, contributing to an independent expenditure committee that’s spent more than $1 million to oppose her.
GOOD MORNING. Happy Monday. Thanks for waking up with California Playbook.

WHERE’S GAVIN? Holding internal meetings.

Californians are being asked to vote "yes" or "no" on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office, would require election officials to verify Californians' U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID.
It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting "yes" would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you're voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting "no" means the process stays is it is - you don't need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans' currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump's unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters.
It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires’ assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.
